newsitem.title: UK: Mark drifts near session lows, eye on Bonn budget.
newsitem.headline: Mark drifts near session lows, eye on Bonn budget.

text.p: The mark softened on the crosses by European midday, though moves were small with the market treading water as it kept an eye on any news concerning the German budget.
The German cabinet was meeting today to discuss Finance Minister Theo Waigel's draft for the 1997 supplementary budget and 1998 budget proposals.

The market's focus of interest was on whether Bonn would be able to meet the three percent budget-deficit-to-GDP target ratio required to join European monetary union, and what measures it planned to take in its efforts to attain that goal.
But traders were not holding their breath, as German government sources had already said on Thursday the 1997 deficit was likely to be 3.0 percent of GDP at 110 billion marks.
"The budget's pretty much been leaked in recent days, and it's not really expected to do a tremendous amount to the market either way," said one trader at a U.S. bank here.

The mark was at 3.3799/04 French francs at 1020 GMT against 3.3796/01 seen in late Thursday European trade and near this morning's lows. Traders cited a bit of profit-taking in mark/Paris after it rose to a one-month high on Thursday.
Analysts said Germany was likely to show in the draft budgets that it would be able to meet the three-percent target one way or another.

Bonn announced its latest deficit-plugging measure on Thursday -- the sale of its stockpile of emergency oil reserves, with the first tranche of the sales this year expected to raise 400 million marks. Government sources said on Friday that Bonn intended to sell all its strategic oil reserves of 7.3 million tonnes by 1999.

"In the end we'll see a small overshoot above three percent. For the time being they'll basically say that despite the overshoot in the federal deficit they'll get to three percent, and not really tell us all the details," said Kay Sinden, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
"But I don't expect them to be introducing any new one-off measures (in the budget)," Sinden said.
In France, central bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet said he believed France's 1997 budget deficit could be reduced but that it would depend on the decisions taken.

Meanwhile, EU Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, in an interview with Britain's Daily Telegraph newspaper, refused to rule out the admission to EMU of nations whose deficits were well above three percent of their GDP.
Elsewhere, the Norwegian central bank raised its fixed-term deposit rate for July 14-17 to 3.8 percent from the 3.7 percent for the preceding five days.
The Norwegian crown was weaker against the mark in choppy trade, quoted at 4.1960/90 per mark compared with Thursday's 4.1855/85.

"The Scandinavian currencies are the only ones moving substantially today, with good sellers of Norway and decent buyers of Swedish crowns. But it's mainly lack of liquidity," said the U.S. bank trader.
